title: Testing I: unittest
subtitle: Prove your code works, and keep it working
goal: Write automated tests with assert and unittest that pin down normal behaviour, edge cases and errors.
outcomes: Explain why professional teams automate their tests
Write TestCase classes with assertion methods and setUp
Structure every test as Arrange, Act, Assert
Test boundaries and expected exceptions with assertRaises
Read a failing test report and go straight to the cause

slides.title: Mission 35: Code that checks code
slides.body:
Every serious codebase has **automated tests**: small programs that check your program.

They catch bugs before users do, let you change code without fear, and document what the code is supposed to do. Many teams won't merge code without them.

items: Write tests that state what it should do
Run every test on every change

slides.say: Every serious codebase has automated tests: small programs whose only job is to check your program. Tests catch bugs before your users do, let you change code without fear, and document exactly how the code should behave. At most companies, code without tests simply does not get merged.

slides.title: Manual checks don't scale
slides.body: Printing a result and eyeballing it works once. A **test** remembers the right answer forever and re-checks it in milliseconds, every time anyone changes anything.

visual.verdict: The assert states the expected answer and checks it on every run.

slides.say: Until now you checked code by printing a result and looking at it. That works once. But next month, when someone changes the discount logic, nobody will remember to look again. A test stores the right answer and re-checks it in milliseconds, every single time the code changes.

slides.title: The simplest test: assert
explain: Edge case: 100% should make it free.
Only reached if every assert passed.
slides.say: An assert statement checks that something is true. If it is, nothing happens and Python moves on. If it is not, the program stops with an assertion error. So silence means success. Here we check a normal discount, a zero percent discount, and a full one hundred percent discount.

slides.title: Predict: the edge case
slides.code:
def is_adult(age):
    return age > 18

assert is_adult(30)
assert is_adult(18), "18 should count as an adult"
print("done")
options: AssertionError: 18 should count as an adult
slides.why: is_adult(18) is False because 18 > 18 is False, so the second assert fails and shows its message. The normal case passed; the edge case found the bug. The fix is >=.
slides.say: Here is a function and two checks. The first is a normal case, the second is the boundary, exactly eighteen. Will this print done? Predict, then run.

slides.title: unittest: tests with structure
slides.body:
Python's built-in `unittest` organises tests into classes:

- inherit from `unittest.TestCase`
- every method named `test_...` is one test
- `self.assertEqual` and friends give clear failure messages

In this app: `unittest.main(argv=['x'], exit=False)`. Its report appears in the error area.
slides.say: For real projects, Python ships a test framework called unittest. You write a class that inherits from test case, and every method whose name starts with test is one test. Assertion methods like assert equal give much clearer failure messages than a bare assert. In this app we call unittest main with two extra arguments so it runs safely inside the page.

slides.title: Your first TestCase
explain: A test class inherits from unittest.TestCase.
Each test_ method is one independent test.
Passes only if the block raises ValueError.
Run all tests in this file; the report goes to the error stream.
testsRun and wasSuccessful() summarise the run.
slides.say: Three tests, each a method with a name that describes one behaviour. The third uses assert raises as a with block: the test passes only if the code inside raises a value error. Unittest finds every test method, runs them, and prints its report of dots and OK in the error area. We also print a short summary from the result object.

slides.title: Assertion methods
slides.body: Pick the assertion that says what you mean. When it fails, unittest shows **both** values.
slides.say: Test case gives you a family of assertions. Assert equal for exact values, assert in for membership, assert is none for missing values, and assert raises for errors. For floats, use assert almost equal, because tiny rounding errors make exact comparisons fail. Choosing the right one makes failure messages tell you exactly what went wrong.

slides.title: Reading a failure
explain: This expectation doesn't match what the code does.
result.failures is a list of (test, report) pairs.
The report's last line shows actual != expected.
slides.say: This time a test fails, and that is useful. The report names the exact test, and the last line shows both values side by side: the function returned thirty three point three recurring, but the test expected two decimals. Now we decide: should the function round to paise, or should the test use assert almost equal? Failing tests start exactly these conversations.

slides.title: Floats in tests
slides.q: Which assertion should check that 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.3?
slides.why: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point, so assertEqual fails. assertAlmostEqual compares to 7 decimal places by default (or places=2 for money).
slides.say: Remember from day three that zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three. Which assertion handles that properly?

slides.title: Arrange, Act, Assert
slides.body:
Every good test has three parts. Keep one behaviour per test, and name it like a sentence: `test_withdraw_more_than_balance_raises`.

`setUp()` runs **before each test**, so every test starts fresh.

items: Arrange: build the objects and inputs
Act: call the one thing you are testing

slides.say: Good tests share a shape called arrange, act, assert. First arrange: build the objects and inputs. Then act: call the one thing you are testing. Then assert: check the result. Name each test like a sentence describing the behaviour. And put shared arranging in set up, which runs before every single test, so no test can disturb another.

slides.title: setUp: a fresh cart for every test
slides.body: The `Cart` class lives in `cart.py`, imported like a real module.
explain: Import the code under test from its module.
setUp runs before every test method.
failures are wrong answers; errors are crashes. Count both.
slides.say: The cart class lives in its own file, like real code. Set up builds a brand new cart before each test, so the items added in one test can never leak into another. Each test then acts once and asserts once. Notice how the test names read like a specification of the cart.

slides.title: Predict: when does setUp run?
slides.why: setUp runs before each test, not once for the class, so every test starts from a clean state. (unittest runs test methods in alphabetical order: test_a, then test_b.)
slides.say: Two tests and a set up method, each appending to a log. When the tests finish, what does the log contain?

slides.title: Hunt for edge cases
slides.body: Bugs live at the edges. For every function, test a normal case, then the boundaries: empty, zero, one, the exact limit, just past it, negative, and invalid input.

head: Function
Normal
Edges worth testing
rows: "", one word, ties, k too big

slides.say: Most bugs live at the edges. Normal cases usually work, because that is what the developer had in mind. So for every function, ask: what about empty input, zero, exactly one item, the exact boundary, one past it, negative numbers and invalid input? Professionals write those tests first.

slides.title: Fix the bug: grade boundaries
slides.task: The tests describe the rules: **90 and above** is A, **75 and above** B, **40 and above** C, below 40 F. Run it, read which test fails, and fix the **function**, not the tests.
slides.tests:
assert 'self.assertEqual(grade(90), "A")' in __code__ and 'self.assertEqual(grade(75), "B")' in __code__, "Keep the tests as they are: fix the grade function instead."
assert grade(90) == "A", f"90 marks should be an A, got {grade(90)!r}. 'And above' means >=."
assert grade(75) == "B", f"75 marks should be a B, got {grade(75)!r}."
assert grade(89) == "B" and grade(74) == "C", "89 is a B and 74 is a C."
assert grade(40) == "C" and grade(39) == "F" and grade(100) == "A", "Check 40 (C), 39 (F) and 100 (A) too."
hints: The report says test_boundaries failed: which line of it, and which value came back?
'90 and above' means marks >= 90. Same for 75.
slides.say: The tests are right and the function is wrong. Run it, read the failure report to see which boundary breaks, then fix the function. Never edit a correct test just to make it pass: that is how bugs reach production.

slides.title: Write tests that catch bugs
slides.task:
`shipping_fee` is correct: **free from ₹500**, otherwise ₹40, negative totals raise `ValueError`. Write **at least 3** tests in `TestShippingFee`.

The checker will secretly swap in **buggy versions** of the function. Your tests must fail for every one of them.
hints: Test the boundary itself: shipping_fee(500) should be 0, and shipping_fee(499) should be 40.
One behaviour per test method, each name starting with test_.
slides.say: Now you are the tester. The function is correct, and your job is to write tests strong enough to catch bugs. When you tap check, we secretly replace the function with three broken versions. If your tests still pass for any of them, they are not strong enough yet. Think about the boundary.

slides.title: Make the suite green
slides.task:
Tests are also a **specification**. Read `TestWallet`, then write the `Wallet` class so every test passes. Don't change the tests.

Also make `pay()` reject zero or negative amounts with `ValueError`, like `top_up()`.
slides.tests:
import unittest as _u
assert "TestWallet" in globals(), "Keep the TestWallet class: it is the specification."
_n = _u.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(TestWallet).countTestCases()
assert _n >= 6, "Don't delete tests from TestWallet: all 6 should still be there."
_r = _u.TestResult()
_u.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(TestWallet).run(_r)
_bad = _r.failures + _r.errors
assert not _bad, f"{len(_bad)} test(s) still fail. First one: {_bad[0][0].id().split('.')[-1]} -> {_bad[0][1].strip().splitlines()[-1]}" if _bad else ""
w = Wallet("Kabir", 50)
for bad in (0, -10):
    try:
        w.pay(bad)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError(f"pay({bad}) should raise ValueError: payments must be positive.")
assert w.balance == 50, "A rejected payment must not change the balance."
w.pay(50)
assert w.balance == 0, "Paying exactly the whole balance is allowed, leaving 0."
hints: Wallet needs __init__(self, owner, balance=0) that stores both attributes.
top_up and pay should raise ValueError for amounts <= 0. pay also raises if amount > self.balance.
Check before you change: raise first, and only then update self.balance.
slides.say: Tests are also a specification. Read the wallet tests carefully: they tell you the constructor, the methods and every rule. Then write the wallet class until the whole suite is green. Don't touch the tests.

slides.title: When a bug escapes
slides.q: All tests pass, but a user reports a bug. What's the professional next step?
options: Fix the bug quickly and move on
Write a test that reproduces the bug, watch it fail, then fix the code
Delete the tests, since they obviously don't work
slides.why: A failing test proves you understood the bug, and once it passes it guards against that bug forever. This habit is called a regression test.
slides.say: Last check. Every test is green, yet a user finds a bug. What should you do before touching the code?

slides.title: Mission 35 complete
points: Automated tests store the right answer and re-check it on every change
unittest: a TestCase class, one test_ method per behaviour, assertEqual and friends
assertRaises checks errors; assertAlmostEqual handles floats
Arrange, Act, Assert; setUp gives every test a fresh start
Test the edges, and turn every bug report into a test first
slides.say: Mission thirty five complete. You can write unittest suites, test edge cases and errors, read failure reports, and write tests strong enough to catch real bugs. Tomorrow we flip the order: tests first, then code, with test driven development and mocks. See you on day thirty six.
